credits.text: Phrases from Omniglot "Useful Shona phrases" (Emma Thembani and Ernest Mdende) and Wiktionary; accuracy-checked, native-speaker review pending.

activities.prompt: Tendai meets Chipo for the first time at a friend's house. Read their exchange in order.

task.feedbackCorrect: Right: Ndinonzi … (My name is …) answers Unonzani?
task.feedbackIncorrect: That answers a different question. Unonzani? asks for your name.
task.prompt: Chipo's cousin asks you "Unonzani?". Which reply fits?

activities.prompt: Say the whole introduction aloud with your own name and home town.

lessons.objective: Follow Tendai and Chipo introducing themselves, then pick the right reply to a name question.
lessons.title: Meeting Chipo

examples: Unonzani? (What are you called?) → Ndinonzi … (I am called …)
Unobva kupi? (Where are you from?) → Ndinobva ku… (I come from …)
activities.explanation: In these two checked pairs the question to one person starts with U- (you) and the answer starts with Ndi- (I). Treat this as a note about these phrases only, not a rule for every Shona verb; that needs a native speaker to confirm.

task.feedbackCorrect: Right: Ndinokumbirawo kuti muzvitaure futi — please say that again.
task.feedbackIncorrect: It opens with the polite request, Ndinokumbirawo, and ends with futi (again).
task.prompt: Ask someone to say it again, politely.

lessons.objective: Notice how a question to you and its answer about me differ in these checked pairs, then build both.
lessons.title: You and I: questions and answers
